question: When a transformer recalls and continues an interleaved dynamical sequence, are the first recalled state and later states predicted by distinct mechanisms, and do those mechanisms emerge at different points in training?

key_findings.claim: Ordinary in-context prediction of an uninterrupted held-out linear dynamical system improves gradually and approaches a pseudoinverse estimator at early context indices.
key_findings.evidence: On 100 held-out systems with 1,000 initial states each, checkpoints after 62.5 million training examples closely match the pseudoinverse at indices two through seven and reach median squared error about 2e-4 late in the context. Test error then rises with further training, motivating early stopping.

anchors.section: 3.2.1 Can a model learn the first system in-context?

key_findings.claim: The ability to restart in-context prediction on a newly introduced system emerges much earlier than associative recall.
key_findings.evidence: Prediction errors in the third newly seen segment converge toward first-segment errors after roughly two million training examples, whereas first-state recall transitions after more than ten million. Some later within-segment indices still degrade as more systems are introduced.

anchors.section: 3.2.2 Emergence of the ability to restart ICL

key_findings.claim: Recall of the first state after a symbolic query label emerges later and more sharply than prediction of subsequent states in the recalled segment.
key_findings.evidence: Across needle-in-a-haystack tests, the first-after-final error drops abruptly after about 15 million examples for one candidate system and roughly 25 million for five, while later-token errors improve earlier and more gradually. At the selected final checkpoint, first-token error remains near 0.015 across haystack size while later-token errors worsen with more systems.

anchors.section: Figure 12 final performance by haystack size

key_findings.claim: Wrong-label misdirection indicates that the first recalled state depends on the symbolic label while predictions two or more states later are nearly label-insensitive in the standard test.
key_findings.evidence: Replacing the final label with one pointing to a different haystack system makes first-state error rise sharply late in training, but the second-, third-, seventh-, and eighth-state curves remain almost identical to the correctly labeled recall curves.

key_findings.claim: The later-token route is suboptimal and cannot simply be called Bayes-optimal observation-based recall.
key_findings.evidence: When all haystack systems are synchronized to the same first recalled state, the label supplies the needed identity, but predictions from the second state onward fail badly. Performance remains poor even after an additional state would disambiguate the generating system, contradicting an optimal Bayesian update.

key_findings.claim: Later predictions are not fully label-agnostic: an unseen label eventually triggers another abrupt transition toward restarting a new sequence.
key_findings.evidence: With a final label absent from the haystack but observations continuing an old system, later-state predictions stay accurate until about 30 million training examples, then second- and third-state errors sharply increase as the model begins treating the label as a new-system signal.

key_findings.claim: When a seen label points to an old system but the observations start a genuinely new system, later predictions restart from observations rather than obeying the label.
key_findings.evidence: For two or more states after the query, error curves match the normal new-system restart experiment even under a previously seen, misleading label; only the first post-label prediction follows the symbolic cue.

key_findings.claim: Edge pruning finds behaviorally selective sparse graphs for first- and second-state prediction, but the reported zero-overlap circuit result is a fragile single-configuration analysis rather than definitive evidence of two disjoint mechanisms.
key_findings.evidence: The 200-edge first-after circuit has squared errors 0.01 on first-after and 0.64 on second-after, while the 40-edge second-after circuit has 0.32 and 0.02; reported edge overlap is 0%. Footnotes disclose one trace configuration, no full train-test split, and an earlier model trained from a nonuniform orthogonal-matrix distribution.

key_findings.claim: OLMo-2 7B translation checkpoints show a similar first-token versus second-token timing gap, but the natural-language validation is only a 100-sample checkpoint probe.
key_findings.evidence: With symbolic X:/Y: task labels, first-token English-to-Spanish accuracy changes sharply around 50,000 steps while second-token accuracy is higher and smoother. Replacing symbolic labels with Spanish:/English: removes the gap. Each checkpoint is evaluated on 100 samples with Jeffreys-prior intervals.

anchors.section: 5 Do Pretrained LLMs Also Display Multi-Mechanism Tendencies?

key_findings.claim: Emergence moves earlier with model size and aligns roughly by held-out pretraining loss, but threshold selection and scale controls are not preregistered or statistically robust.
key_findings.evidence: Four sizes from 212K to 10.7M parameters show earlier transitions for larger models, using error cutoffs 0.4 and 0.5 selected by visual inspection. First-state recall clusters near pretraining loss 0.065 and second-state recall above 0.1, but learning rate, batch size, hardware, and sometimes data family vary with size.

anchors.section: 6.1 Training dynamics with respect to pretraining loss

method.core_idea: Train a small transformer on symbolically labeled, randomly interleaved segments from many linear dynamical systems, then use token-position-resolved learning curves, adversarial inference-time recombinations, and sparse circuit discovery to separate label-based recall from observation-based continuation.
method.mechanism: Each training trace interleaves segments from a fixed library of 40,000 five-dimensional orthogonal systems, with a fresh random label pair for each system in every example. A 12-layer GPT-2-style model predicts continuous states under mean-squared error while label-token losses are masked. Needle-in-a-haystack tests query one prior segment. Four OOD manipulations independently change labels, observations, and system identity; edge pruning searches sparse component graphs for first- versus second-state prediction. OLMo-2 7B checkpoints provide a small translation analogue.
assumptions: Randomly reassigned symbolic labels force associations to be learned within each context rather than memorized in weights.
Five-dimensional noiseless orthogonal dynamics are a useful proxy for continuous in-context learning and recall.
A pseudoinverse estimator is the relevant observation-based benchmark for uninterrupted local dynamics.
Prediction position within a recalled segment can isolate distinct computational requirements.
OOD recombinations preserve enough task semantics that behavioral failures identify which information source the model uses.
Sparse edge-pruned subnetworks faithfully reveal the computation used by the original model after gate quantization.
A first-versus-second-token translation gap is meaningfully analogous to first-state retrieval versus continuation in the toy task.
Median and configuration-quartile squared errors adequately summarize the highly structured test set.

techniques.role: Prevents stable in-weights label meanings while creating repeated-sequence recall opportunities.
Controls the number and position of candidate systems in a long recall context.
Separates first recalled state, later continuation states, and new-system restart behavior during training.
Tests whether prediction follows the symbolic query or observed dynamics.
Removes the identifying information in the first recalled observation while preserving label information.
Distinguishes a generic new-label restart signal from a precise retrieved-system identity.
Searches sparse transformer computation graphs separately for consecutive prediction positions.
Tests whether a first-versus-second-token timing gap appears in OLMo translation training.

evaluations.setting: Uninterleaved held-out orthogonal systems: 100 systems times 1,000 initial states
evaluations.metric: Median next-state squared error by context index and training examples
evaluations.result: Approaches the pseudoinverse on early indices by 62.5M examples and reaches about 2e-4 late-context error before overfitting

evaluations.setting: Needle-in-a-haystack recall with 1-19 systems, 50 configurations, and 1,000 initial states per system
evaluations.metric: Median and interquartile squared error by token position and training checkpoint
evaluations.result: First-state recall emerges later and more abruptly than continuation; first-state final error stays near 0.015 while later errors rise with haystack size
evaluations.baseline: Corresponding positions after the initial label and pseudoinverse prediction

evaluations.result: First-state prediction follows labels; continuation is mainly observation-driven, suboptimal under synchronization, but can respond to unseen-label restart signals late in training
evaluations.baseline: Unmodified recall and new-system restart traces

evaluations.setting: Edge pruning on a five-system trace configuration
evaluations.metric: Post-quantization edge count, cross-task squared error, and edge overlap
evaluations.result: 200-edge first-state and 40-edge second-state circuits are selective and have reported 0% overlap
evaluations.baseline: 32,936-edge full model with 0.002 and 0.004 task errors

evaluations.setting: OLMo-2 7B English-to-Spanish prompting across training checkpoints
evaluations.metric: First- and second-token accuracy with 95% Jeffreys credible intervals
evaluations.result: Symbolic labels produce a first-token jump near 50K steps while second-token accuracy grows earlier; semantic labels erase the gap
evaluations.baseline: Spanish:/English: labels and second-token accuracy; 100 samples per point

evaluations.setting: Four toy-model scales from 212K to 10.7M parameters
evaluations.metric: Transition checkpoint and held-out pretraining loss
evaluations.result: Larger models transition earlier in examples seen; approximate alignment occurs near loss 0.065 for first-state and above 0.1 for second-state recall
evaluations.baseline: Visually selected task-error cutoffs and pseudoinverse pretraining-loss lower bound

limitations: The task is noiseless, five-dimensional, and restricted mainly to orthogonal or identity dynamics, so its Bayesian and recall structure is unusually tractable.
Training interleavings are fresh but draw from a fixed library of 40,000 systems, allowing repeated underlying dynamics across examples.
Only one main training run per setting is foregrounded; seed and hyperparameter uncertainty for emergence timing is not reported.
The 62.5M-example checkpoint is selected after observing held-out overfitting.
Needle tests use 50 overlapping ordered configurations and report quartiles over configuration medians, not independent system-family replications.
The observation-based route is called Bayesian-style behaviorally but no explicit likelihood, posterior, or circuit computation is recovered.
The edge-pruning result uses one trace configuration, lacks a full train-test split, and comes from an earlier nonuniform-system training run.
Zero edge overlap between separately thresholded circuits does not establish that the full model has exactly two independent mechanisms.
Model-size comparisons change learning rate, batch size, hardware, and sometimes data family; emergence cutoffs are chosen by visual inspection.
The OLMo translation analogue has only 100 samples per checkpoint and no circuit or OOD mechanism analysis.
Losses on special label tokens are masked, which shapes how symbolic information can be learned and used.
The paper demonstrates at least two routes for this task, not a universal decomposition of natural-language ICL.
failure_modes: A local observation shortcut can work on ordinary recall traces yet fail when multiple candidate systems share the same immediate state.
A symbolic label can trigger generic restart behavior without accurately retrieving the labeled system.
Late training can overfit the fixed dynamics library even as training loss continues to improve.
First-token and later-token errors can differ because of task information structure rather than separable learned circuits.
A pruned circuit can be selective only on the one configuration used to optimize its gates.
Thresholding continuous gates can create artificial disjointness between circuits with distributed or redundant shared computation.
Changing label semantics can let in-weights knowledge bypass the intended in-context recognition requirement.
Scale trends can be confounded by learning-rate, batch-size, hardware, and data-generation changes.
Median error can hide rare catastrophic retrieval failures as the haystack grows.
A translation tokenizer or target-word morphology can make the first token intrinsically harder than the second independent of recall mechanism.
reusable_insights: Evaluate multi-token capabilities separately at the first decision token and at continuation tokens; aggregate sequence accuracy can hide distinct routes.
Use counterfactual combinations of labels and observations to distinguish information-source dependence from mere task performance.
Synchronizing candidate states is a strong test of whether a model can integrate an explicit identifier with local dynamics rather than follow a shortcut.
A mechanism described as Bayesian should be tested on cases where one more observation makes the posterior identifiable.
A new-label response and correct label-conditioned retrieval are different capabilities and should be factored experimentally.
Circuit discovery should use family-held-out configurations, repeated seeds, behavior-preserving controls, and overlap uncertainty before asserting disjoint mechanisms.
Checkpointed pretrained models can test whether toy-task temporal predictions transfer, but the analogy needs matched information structure and tokenization controls.
Emergence claims should preregister thresholds and control optimization dose before comparing scale.
open_questions: Can a controlled intervention make later-state prediction use the symbolic label and thereby repair the synchronization failure?
Is the later route an approximate system-identification algorithm, a nearest-history heuristic, or another recoverable computation?
How many mechanisms are needed when labels, observations, noise, and dynamics ambiguity are varied factorially?
Do the first- and second-state circuits remain disjoint across random seeds, trace families, haystack positions, and pruning targets?
Can causal activation patching or compiled ground-truth models validate the edge-pruning interpretation?
Does the phase ordering persist for noisy, nonlinear, nonorthogonal, partially observed, or previously unseen system families?
Can a frozen loss threshold predict mechanism emergence prospectively at a held-out larger model scale?
Does the OLMo first-token gap survive languages with matched tokenization, prompt paraphrases, more samples, and causal circuit tests?
How does masking label-token loss affect emergence and information routing?
Can training curricula prevent the easy continuation route from suppressing a globally correct label-integrating route?

competitive_landscape.title: Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Zoology formalizes multi-query associative recall, ties recall gaps to natural-language perplexity, and compares attention with gated convolutions. The target combines associative labels with continuous system identification and decomposes prediction by position and mechanism rather than architecture efficiency.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. associate induction-head formation with a training phase change and give causal evidence for match-and-copy in small attention-only models. The target finds position-specific routes in a continuous recall task and argues the continuation route is not simple symbolic match-and-copy.

competitive_landscape.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
competitive_landscape.difference: This work tracks uniform, unigram, and bigram phases and explains statistical induction-head formation on Markov chains. The target studies a single composite task whose first and continuation positions develop differently, using OOD interventions and pruning rather than a full training-dynamics theory.

competitive_landscape.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: ICLL studies regular-language generation and higher-order n-gram heads across multiple architectures, with a natural-text architectural intervention. The target instead uses labeled interleaved dynamics to isolate task recognition from local continuation at consecutive output positions.

competitive_landscape.title: Competition Dynamics Shape Algorithmic Phases of In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Competition Dynamics decomposes one Markov-mixture model into four retrieval/inference and unigram/bigram algorithms whose dominance changes with context and training. The target's novelty is token-position-resolved counterfactual evidence within one recall episode, but its two-route description is less algorithmically explicit.

competitive_landscape.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Strategy Coopetition identifies shared subcircuits and competitive/cooperative learning between ICL and context-constrained in-weights learning. The target reports disjoint pruned graphs for consecutive tokens, but on a single fragile pruning setup and without a dynamics model of circuit interaction.

competitive_landscape.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
competitive_landscape.difference: Wei et al. show scale changes whether LMs follow in-context input-label mappings or semantic priors, including semantically unrelated labels. The target randomizes label meanings in a toy dynamical task and separates label use at the first versus later output positions.

competitive_landscape.title: Dual Operating Modes of In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Dual Operating Modes derives a posterior split between retrieving a pretrained skill and learning a task from context. The target's labels are reassigned every example, so its first route performs within-context recognition while its later route identifies dynamics from observations; no closed-form risk theory is supplied.

competitive_landscape.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
competitive_landscape.difference: This work uses activation clamping through training to identify three additive subcircuits that causally enable induction-head phase change. The target uses inference-time counterfactuals and post hoc edge pruning; it does not causally manipulate route formation during training.

competitive_landscape.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
competitive_landscape.relationship: methodological foundation and competing circuit comparison
competitive_landscape.difference: Bhaskar et al. introduce scalable edge pruning, validate exact recovery on Tracr, and find highly sparse instruction-prompting and ICL circuits with substantial overlap in CodeLlama-13B. The target adapts the method to squared error and reports zero overlap, but only for one trace configuration and a mismatched earlier toy-model run.

competitive_landscape.title: Context-Gated Associative Retrieval: From Theory to Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: This later work proposes a two-stage context-gate and retrieval feedback circuit, proves improved separation and a unique fixed point, and tests a first-order approximation on Llama-3. The target supplies training-time phase separation and tokenwise OOD evidence but no formal retrieval-energy or fixed-point theory.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A single in-context recall task is solved by at least two separate mechanisms with different learning dynamics: label-based prediction for the first recalled token and largely label-agnostic Bayesian-style prediction for continuation, with a similar phase split in OLMo translation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Token-position learning curves, four label-observation counterfactuals, selective pruned circuits, and checkpointed translation tests all separate first-state prediction from later continuation behavior.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the conjunction of a continuous-dynamics plus symbolic-recall toy task, token-position-resolved training trajectories, and OOD interventions that show label and observation routes can disagree within one resumed segment. Associative-recall benchmarks, induction heads, multi-algorithm ICL, task recognition versus learning, symbolic-label scale effects, causal circuit-formation studies, and edge-pruning comparisons already exist. The evidence supports at least two behaviorally distinct routes in this setup, not exactly two universal or disjoint mechanisms: the later route is not Bayes-optimal, unseen labels affect it, the zero-overlap pruning result is underpowered and model-mismatched, and the OLMo analogue is only a small behavioral probe.
